summary.text: Oscillation is a repeating variation of some quantity around a central value, such as the swing of a pendulum or the flow of alternating current.
It happens when a system displaced from equilibrium feels a restoring force that pulls it back, while its momentum carries it past the middle again.
Real oscillators lose energy as heat through friction or resistance, so their swings fade unless something keeps feeding them energy.

facts.label: Mechanical name
facts.value: A mechanical oscillation is called a vibration

facts.label: Simplest system
facts.value: A weight attached to a spring

facts.label: Oscillatory period
facts.value: The time one full oscillation takes

facts.label: Driven oscillation
facts.value: Pushed by an outside force, like an AC circuit on a power source

items.prompt: You pull a toy on a spring downward and let go. It bounces up past its resting height. What carries it past that point?

options.label: The restoring force stays strongest at the middle
Gravity switches direction at the middle
The momentum it gained on the way back
The spring stops pulling at the middle

items.explain: Moving back toward equilibrium gives the mass momentum, which keeps it going past that point and sets up a new restoring force the other way.

items.prompt: A weight hangs from a spring. You then hang a second, heavier load that adds a constant downward pull. What happens to the middle of the bounce?

options.label: It shifts to a new equilibrium point
It stays at the same spot
It disappears and the bouncing stops
It splits into two middle points

items.explain: A constant force such as gravity moves the point of equilibrium, and the oscillation happens around the new point.

items.prompt: A swing is pushed once and then left alone. Over several minutes, its swings get smaller. Which idea explains this best?

options.label: The swing runs out of restoring force
Friction turns some of its energy into heat
The period gets longer and stops it
Its momentum is gradually deleted

items.explain: Real oscillators have dissipative processes that convert stored energy into heat, so oscillations decay unless energy is supplied.

items.prompt: A bridge engineer notes that a perfectly frictionless spring-and-weight model would never stop moving. What property of the model explains that?

options.label: The weight has no momentum
The spring never reaches equilibrium
Gravity keeps adding energy
Nothing removes energy, so the wave never shrinks

items.explain: The cosine describing the motion swings between its positive and negative limits forever, so without friction the system would oscillate indefinitely.

items.prompt: A spring pulls back harder the farther you stretch it. Why is this feature central to oscillation?

options.label: A bigger stretch always returns the mass sooner
A bigger pull cancels out the momentum
A growing pull toward the middle keeps the motion centred on equilibrium
A bigger stretch removes the need for equilibrium

items.explain: Equilibrium plus a restoring force that grows with distance from it are common features of oscillating systems.

items.prompt: A machine's valve flutters rapidly and the control engineers want it to settle. How do they view that oscillation?

options.label: As unwanted, since the aim is a stable state
As ideal, since it shows equilibrium
As a sign of perfect efficiency
As a harmless route to a bigger swing

items.explain: In process control, rapid oscillation can be undesirable because the goal is convergence to a stable state; it is called chattering.
